About me

It started in third grade, when my grandparents gave me a Snap Circuits set for Christmas. I couldn’t stop wondering how it worked, so I kept digging deeper into how it all fit together. Over the years, that early curiosity grew into a real interest in circuits, electronic boards, and anything I can build with my hands. It is what drives me to become the engineer I want to be today. On the design side, I have worked with CAD tools including Onshape, Revit, SolidWorks, AutoCAD, and Inventor, and I know the basics of Python.

I was selected for a three-week leadership program at Woodlands Camp, a summer camp. I served meals three times a day, worked free-time shifts, and did a lot of behind-the-scenes work around camp. It asked a lot of me, and I had to draw on strength I did not know I had. Through that experience, I learned what a strong work ethic really looks like in practice. The lessons I learned there are still some of the most useful ones I know. That kind of responsibility was not new to me. For three years, I was a confirmation leader at my church, guiding middle school small groups of 5 to 15 kids, and in my third year I was chosen to lead the other leaders. Before camp, I also spent more than two years at Chick-fil-A, where I was trusted as the lead breader.

Outside of class, I love serving others, going to church, spending time with friends, and staying active through sports. I am part of the CanSat Robotics Club, where I work with a team on a glider, and I am a member of the Theta Xi fraternity. Working with other people on hands-on engineering is the kind of work I want to keep doing, and I’m looking to bring that same energy to a co-op starting in spring 2028.

Career goals

Long term: In ten years, I want to hold a leadership position at an engineering firm, where I can guide others through meaningful conversations and intentional leadership while working toward innovation. I want to help a team do its best work and still stay close enough to the engineering to push new ideas forward.

Here is how I plan to get there:

  1. Fall 2026: build the foundationMy first semester at Georgia Tech includes the ECE Discovery Practicum, Introduction to Computing, Integral Calculus, Principles of Physics I, and First Year Seminar. I also arrived with 30 transfer credits.
  2. Spring 2027 to Fall 2027: math, physics, and digital designI will take Fundamentals of Digital System Design, Linear Algebra, Chemistry, Physics II, Multivariable Calculus, and Differential Equations. These courses give me the tools I need for circuits and electronics.
  3. Spring 2028 to Summer 2029: co-opI plan to start a co-op in spring 2028, continue it in fall 2028, and finish it in summer 2029. Three work terms will let me apply what I have learned in a real engineering setting. My roadmap currently lists courses in spring and fall 2028, so I will move those courses to other semesters around the co-op.
  4. Circuits and devices courseworkAround my co-op terms, I will take Circuit Analysis, Microelectronic Circuits, Electromagnetics, Analog Electronics, and Semiconductor Devices, along with the related laboratories. My thread choices are Circuits and Electronic Devices. I will work with my advisor to place these courses in the right order.
  5. Fall 2029 to graduation: senior yearAfter my co-op, I plan to take Digital Integrated Circuits, Integrated Circuit Fabrication, and ECE Culminating Design I, then graduate in 2030.
  6. After graduation: take on more responsibilityI want to keep growing as a team member and as a leader, starting with teams like CanSat, so that I am ready to take on more responsibility and eventually lead others at an engineering firm.

Discovery Project

Technical projects

BatChair: cardboard rocking chair (TSA)

Cardboard · friction-fit joints · team of four

For the Technology Student Association (TSA) state competition in my junior year of high school, my team of four designed and built a rocking chair made entirely of cardboard, with no other materials. I brainstormed design ideas, developed our build plan, tracked our daily progress, and cut and assembled the cardboard. We used friction-fit joints so the structure held together on its own, which kept the chair sturdy.

The chair rocked while supporting more than 50 pounds, meeting the challenge requirements. The design resembled Batman, so we named it the BatChair.

CO2 race car

Onshape · balsa wood · band saw · spray paint · CO2 power

In my engineering class, I designed and built a CO2-powered race car. I began with 3D sketches, then built a CAD model in Onshape. I shaped the body to minimize aerodynamic drag and mass while meeting the class specifications for body shape and axle spacing. I fabricated the balsa wood body with a band saw and finished it with spray paint. The car then competed head to head on a track with guide strings.

The car did not win its head-to-head race, but I carried the project from concept sketches through CAD modeling and fabrication to a race-ready build.

Medieval mini golf hole

Onshape · 3D printing · laser engraving

In a class project, I independently designed and built one hole of a medieval-themed mini golf course. I modeled three obstacles in Onshape and 3D printed them: a miniature castle, a stone with a retractable sword, and a torch with a lit flame on top. I laser engraved the wood base and sides to fit the layout of the hole. The printed obstacles were painted, and fake grass was added on top of the wooden layout.

The finished hole combined 3D printed, laser engraved, and hand-finished parts into one themed design.

Revit house design and physical model

Revit · paper model

I used Revit to design a two-story house adaptable to outdoor settings. The design includes an indoor half-court basketball court, a game room, a living room, a kitchen, a dining room, an outdoor pool, and a garage. We then built a physical model of the house, including both stories, from a thin paper material.

I carried the design from a digital Revit model to a finished physical model.
